## Introduction

The companion post to this essay — [*The Architecture of Focus*](/posts/post-with-code/Consideration_Sets_Attention/attention.qmd) — took 13 days and 18 commits. It started as a technical comparison between transformer attention and econometric consideration sets, with bias detection as the motivating question. It ended as an argument about accountability infrastructure: how the architecture of multi-head attention functions as what Dan Davies calls an *accountability sink*, and how consideration set models provide a counter-architecture with named parameters, posteriors, and an exclusion restriction you can argue about.

The core analogy was there from the first draft. Everything else — the rhetorical structure, the real-data empirical grounding, the political framing — emerged through iterative dialogue with an AI system (Claude). This essay maps that evolution. Not as a guide to AI-assisted writing. There are enough of those. Rather, it is a record of how an argument changes shape when you refine it collaboratively with a system that can diagnose technical failures, recognise structural patterns across domains, and execute editorial passes at speed.

![The argument evolved through six phases, from technical analogy to accountability infrastructure.](argument_arc.png)

## The Initial Draft

The first commit landed on March 13: ~1,200 lines containing the Q/K/V ↔ consideration set structural map, the Linda conjunction fallacy as a motivating example, and four working transformer demos (static attention, learned attention, the conjunction fallacy probe, and multi-head distribution). The bias focus was explicit from the start. The structural analogy table was there. The four demos worked.

What was missing was not content but *argument*. The post had machinery — working code, correct maths, a clean analogy table — but no rhetorical thread. No metaphor to carry the reader through. No real-world data to ground the synthetic validation. No political framing to connect the technical observation to anything a regulator or policymaker would care about.

Over the next five days, the econometric side was built out. The starting point was my earlier work on mixed logit models using PyMC Marketing — I supplied the implementation pattern, and the dialogue extended it to handle the consideration set decomposition. A hiring DGP, a PyMC consideration set model, posterior interpretation, a side-by-side comparison visualisation. The first tightening pass removed 140 lines. By March 18, the post had both halves of the analogy working and a concrete bias-detection result. But it still read like a technical report.

![18 commits over 13 days. The Swiss Metro addition is the steepest spike; the tightening passes are the dips.](line_evolution.png)

## The Surrogate Likelihood

One technical discovery during this phase was genuinely new to me. The structural consideration set model says each alternative is independently in or out of the consideration set, generating $2^J$ possible subsets. You marginalise over all of them to get the choice probability. For three alternatives that's manageable. For ten it is not.

The log-consideration-adjusted utility (Swait & Ben-Akiva, 1987; Cascetta & Papola, 2001) collapses the combinatorial sum into a single softmax:

$$P(j \text{ chosen}) \approx \text{softmax}_j\!\bigl(\log \pi_{nj} + V_{nj}\bigr)$$

The log-consideration probability $\log \pi_{nj}$ and the utility $V_{nj}$ simply *add* inside the softmax. The hard-gating structural story motivates the decomposition — each alternative is in the set or not — but the reduced form makes it estimable. This is a surrogate likelihood, not the structural model. The distinction matters: we are not estimating latent binary gates. We are estimating a tractable approximation that is identified under the exclusion restriction and sufficient for the audit question.

I had not encountered this trick before the research for this post. The additive collapse is elegant: it preserves the two-stage interpretive structure (screening then evaluation) while avoiding the combinatorial explosion. It is also what makes the transformer analogy precise — $\log \pi_{nj}$ plays the role of the query-key dot product, $V_{nj}$ is the value, and both enter a softmax. The parallel is not just structural but operational: both frameworks add a relevance score to a payload inside a normalising function.

Understanding the surrogate likelihood also clarified what the model *cannot* do. It cannot recover the latent consideration sets themselves. It recovers the *marginal effect* of each instrument on the consideration-adjusted choice probability. That is enough for audit — you can say "$\gamma_z$ for race is large and positive for Firm C, meaning race strongly gates consideration at that firm" — but it is not a structural estimate of who was actually considered. The distinction between the structural story and the estimable surrogate became a recurring theme in the post, and getting it right early shaped every modelling decision that followed.

## Finding a Voice

On March 23, the AI dialogue began in earnest. The first prompt asked for an assessment of writing style and redundancy through the lens of Deirdre McCloskey — the economist whose *Economical Writing* argues that academics write badly because they hedge, pad, and refuse to commit to a claim.

The AI executed the prose tightening: splitting run-on sentences, cutting throat-clearing ("It is important to note that..."), replacing passive constructions. But the more interesting contribution was structural. The streetlight image had been added to the post but sat disconnected — an illustration without an argument. The dialogue produced a way to make it argue:

> *The old joke about searching under the streetlight applies here. Interpretability tools examine attention weights because they are visible, not because they are where the bias lives. Single-head attention is the lamppost: you can see the weights clearly, so you look there. Multi-head attention scatters the keys into the dark. Consideration set models do something different. They ask not where does the mechanism put the bias? but does the system's behaviour exhibit bias, and on which variables? They bring their own light.*

The streetlight was then threaded through three touch-points: the introduction (lamppost = single-head), the multi-head interpretability callout ("The keys are in the dark"), and the conclusion ("They do not search under the lamppost"). A disconnected image became a structural metaphor that carried the argument.

::: {.callout-note icon=false}
## Before and after

**Before**: "These systems encode bias. They learn it from data generated by biased human decisions. The real problem is detection: can we *locate and quantify* what they encode? Consideration set models separate 'who gets noticed' from 'who gets chosen.' They provide the audit infrastructure that transformer attention lacks."

**After**: "These systems encode bias. They learn it from data generated by biased human decisions. The real problem is detection. Can we *locate and quantify* what they encode? Consideration set models separate 'who gets noticed' from 'who gets chosen.' They provide the audit infrastructure that transformer attention lacks."

The colon becomes a full stop. "The real problem is detection" becomes a declaration, not a throat-clearing prelude. The question that follows now has force — it lands as a challenge, not a subordinate clause. McCloskey's point: if you believe it, say it. Let the reader decide whether to agree.
:::

## The Aliasing Problem and the Exclusion Restriction

The Swiss Metro dataset was added on March 23. The idea was to move beyond synthetic data validation: nobody hands you the true $\gamma_z$ in the real world. The Swiss Metro survey gives you three transport modes (Train, Swiss Metro, Car), mode-level attributes (time, cost), and person-level characteristics (GA pass, business trip, income, age). The question: which person-level characteristics gate *consideration* of a mode, as distinct from the attributes that drive utility conditional on consideration?

The first model produced a paradoxical result. The GA pass — an annual rail pass — showed *negative* $\gamma_z$ on rail modes. Rail-pass holders appeared to *less* consider rail. The implementation was too simple: it had no consideration intercepts, so the model had to absorb baseline consideration into the utility constants $\alpha_j$. The $\gamma_z$ slopes then picked up the residual with a flipped sign. A specification error, not a deep puzzle.

But diagnosing that specification error exposed something worth writing about. The surrogate likelihood adds $\log \pi_{nj}$ and $V_{nj}$ inside the same softmax. If both components include intercept-like terms — a baseline consideration $\gamma_0$ and a utility constant $\alpha_j$ — those terms compete during sampling. The sampler can shift probability mass between the two without changing the likelihood, because what matters for choice probabilities is only their sum. This is the aliasing problem: consideration intercepts and utility constants are weakly identified against each other unless the instruments do clean separation work.

The GA pass makes the aliasing acute because it is an *impure instrument*. It plausibly shifts both consideration (whether you bother checking car timetables) and utility (rail trips are free at the margin). With no consideration intercept, the model has nowhere to put baseline consideration, so $\alpha_j$ absorbs it and distorts the slopes. With the intercept added, the slopes become interpretable — but the identification is approximate, because the intercept and $\alpha_j$ are aliased in principle even if they are separated in practice by the prior and the data.

The real discovery was not "add an intercept and it works." It was that the aliasing between consideration and utility phases is the central modelling tension in this class of models. The exclusion restriction — the requirement that $Z$ affects consideration but not utility — is what breaks the aliasing. When the instrument is clean, the decomposition is identified. When it is impure, the model can still estimate *something*, but the decomposition is approximate and the intercepts absorb the ambiguity.

The hiring case, by contrast, has *clean* instruments. Protected characteristics like race and age gate whether a résumé is read but should not determine job performance conditional on reading. The upgraded hiring DGP — with a per-firm gamma matrix showing that Firm A screens on both grad degree and race, Firm B screens heavily on grad but weakly on race, Firm C screens heavily on race — makes the clean-instrument case richer and more actionable. You can identify *which firm* screens on *which variable* and intervene. The aliasing problem barely arises because the exclusion restriction holds by construction (and, in practice, by law).

This contrast — clean instruments in hiring where the aliasing is resolved, impure instruments in transport where it persists — became the heart of the argument. But it took multiple rounds to state it properly. The exclusion restriction was always there technically. Its status as the *central modelling choice* only emerged through iterative refinement. The most important idea in the post was latent for several drafts before the right framing surfaced it:

> *The "should not" is not a pious hope; it is the content of anti-discrimination law. When the exclusion restriction and the legal standard say the same thing, the modelling assumption is as defensible as it gets.*

## The Political Turn

The post had argued from the start that multi-head attention distributes bias across anonymous subspaces where it resists audit. That is already a claim about accountability — it just hadn't been named as one. Dan Davies's concept of an *accountability sink* gave the observation its proper name: an institutional structure that absorbs blame without assigning it. Multi-head attention is exactly that for bias. The discrimination is real. No single head is responsible. Calling this an accountability sink is not adding a political frame from outside. It is following the technical observation to its logical conclusion.

The dialogue then extended the logic. The prompt pushed further:

> *Not only is the architecture at risk of obscuring information and responsibility. Eager adoption of these architectures via API calls to vendor LLMs is a pattern of off-loading responsibility to SOTA models rather than human actors or firms...*

The response articulated the three-level nesting:

> *When a firm replaces its screening committee with an API call to a vendor LLM, it outsources the decision and the accountability. The vendor says: "we provide a tool, not a decision." The firm says: "we used the best available technology." The candidate has no one to appeal to. The architecture distributes blame internally across anonymous heads. The procurement structure distributes it externally across organisations.*

The architecture (no single head), the procurement (no single firm), the history (no single decision-maker). Each layer is an accountability sink nested inside the next. The framing was new. The logic was already latent in the post's technical claims. The dialogue surfaced it.

## Craft and Convergence

The final phase was the least dramatic but still necessary. A unified colour palette replaced the ad hoc hex values scattered across 15 plotting cells. Code cells were folded by default. The hiring DGP was upgraded with a per-firm gamma matrix, making the clean-instrument case richer: Firm A screens on both grad degree and race, Firm B screens heavily on grad but weakly on race, Firm C screens heavily on race but weakly on grad. The model recovers the per-firm pattern. You can identify *which firm* screens on *which variable* and intervene.

But the real change in this phase was rhetorical: the exclusion restriction finally moved from technical footnote to argumentative spine. The hiring/Swiss Metro contrast was sharpened. The framework's value was stated not as "it always decomposes cleanly" but as "it makes the decomposition *arguable*." The exclusion restriction is the named assumption you can defend or attack.

Convergence on *what matters* took longer than convergence on *how to say it*. The prose was tight by Phase 3. The argument only landed in Phase 6.

![Per-commit additions (green) and deletions (red). The best commits often remove material.](additions_deletions.png)

## What I Learned

The AI is best as a *respondent*. It needs something to react to. The blank-page problem is not solved. But the "I have a draft and it's not quite right" problem is where the collaboration excels. The iterative rhythm matters: prompt, response, critique, revision. Each cycle tightened the argument.

The most valuable contributions from the dialogue were *structural*. Threading a metaphor across three touch-points. Connecting an institutional concept (accountability sinks) to an architectural property (multi-head attention) to a procurement pattern (vendor APIs). Diagnosing an identification failure in a Bayesian model (the GA paradox). These emerged from the interaction, not from either participant alone.

Letting the AI see failures produced better results than only showing successes. The GA reversal — the most persuasive moment in the finished post — emerged from a modelling failure that was diagnosed collaboratively. If the first model had worked cleanly, the argument would have been weaker: a clean parameter recovery is less convincing than a failure that is diagnosed, fixed, and explained.

The political dimension — accountability sinks, vendor APIs, the chain of delegation — was not planned from the start. It emerged through dialogue. The exclusion restriction as the argumentative spine was latent from Phase 4 but only surfaced in Phase 6. Both observations suggest that iterative refinement discovers emphasis, not just polish. The argument you end up making may not be the argument you set out to make.

The risk is real: fluency without depth. The AI can make anything *sound* right. The human's job is to know when it *is* right. That judgement cannot be delegated. But within that constraint, the collaboration produced something neither participant would have produced alone.

The workflow had an arc I did not anticipate. The essay began as a blog post exploring an analogy. The modelling work — extending my earlier PyMC Marketing mixed logit implementation to handle the consideration set decomposition — turned out to be more than an illustration. The aliasing problem, the exclusion restriction, the surrogate likelihood: working through these in prose clarified what the code needed to do. The essay culminated in a [pull request to pymc-marketing](https://github.com/pymc-labs/pymc-marketing/pull/2442) combining consideration set modelling with mixed logit models. Writing the post was not a detour from the software work. It was the process by which the software design became clear.
